"Reasonable people will not resist the law violently, unless the consequences of resisting the law are no worse than obeying the law, thus desperate...."

- UNLESS the consequences of resisting are no worse than obeying
- Thus, they only desperately resist when the consequences of resistance are no worse than obedience

In logical form:
- If consequences of resisting ≥ consequences of obeying → reasonable people might resist violently
- If consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying → reasonable people will NOT resist violently

Or equivalently:
- Reasonable people violently resist → consequences of resisting ≤ consequences of obeying
- If consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying → reasonable people will NOT violently resist

This says: Rational people will resist violently ONLY IF consequences of resisting ≤ consequences of obeying.

This matches the original! The original says they won't resist unless the consequences are no worse, which means they'll only resist if consequences are no worse.

**B.** "If the consequences of violent resistance to the law are worse than obedience to the law, rational people will not desperately violently resist the law."

This says: If consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying → rational people will NOT resist violently.

This matches the original! The original says they won't resist unless consequences are no worse, so if consequences are worse, they won't resist.

**C.** "If the consequences of obeying the law are better than violent resistance, the rational person will not desperately violently resist the law."

This says: If consequences of obeying > consequences of resisting → rational people will NOT resist violently.

When examining the logical structure, option D emerges as the incongruent statement, as it does not complete the conditional reasoning present in the other options.
